title: Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents
gist: Multiverse Computing researchers present ProvenanceGuard, a post-generation verifier for MCP-based agents that checks not just whether a claim is supported but whether it is supported by the source the answer cites ('cross-source conflation'); on 361 expert-labelled medical claims it caught 138 of 139 bad claims, beat MiniCheck/RAGAS/AlignScore/SummaC on block F1 (0.802), and its approach has been adopted in NVIDIA NVFlow's finance agent.

insights.claim: As tool-using agents combine outputs from multiple MCP tools, a key failure mode is cross-source conflation: a claim true somewhere in the evidence but attributed to the wrong source.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Defines a new reliability problem for enterprise agent deployments that existing evaluation tools miss.
insights.quote: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source.

insights.claim: Most existing answer checkers, including RAGAS faithfulness, MiniCheck, AlignScore and SummaC, judge support against pooled evidence and do not identify which MCP tool output supports each claim.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Incumbent eval tooling has a gap that creates room for source-aware verification products.
insights.locator: Tool-using LLM agents no longer read

insights.claim: In data-sensitive settings a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact, e.g. a policy-document refund window presented as coming from an account record, or a patient-history detail presented as medical-literature evidence.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Attribution errors carry compliance and liability risk in regulated sectors like healthcare and finance.
insights.quote: in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact.

insights.claim: The authors argue that as agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the source of a fact becomes part of what factuality means.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Implies demand shift in AI evaluation/guardrail markets toward provenance tracking.
insights.quote: the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means.

insights.claim: ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation layer over a black-box MCP agent that reads captured tool traces with source IDs, decomposes answers into claims, routes each to a source, checks support, compares against the named source and emits per-claim verdicts plus an allow/block decision, without retraining the agent.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Bolt-on verification that needs no agent retraining lowers adoption friction for enterprises.

insights.claim: The evaluated configuration used local models: MiniLM for source routing, a DeBERTa NLI verifier for support checks, and a local language model for claim decomposition, plus strict literal checks on numbers, dates and identifiers.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Small local models enable offline verification where sensitive traces cannot leave controlled environments.
insights.quote: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible.

insights.claim: Blocked answers can pass through a RARR-style repair loop that attempts a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback before re-verification.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Repair loops turn guardrails from pure blockers into usable production components.

insights.claim: The authors say the approach can be adapted to hosted cloud models, but any new setup would require its own testing and calibration, and reported results come only from the local configuration.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Portability claims are unvalidated beyond the tested stack.
insights.quote: a new setup would need its own testing and calibration.

insights.claim: On a held-out set of 361 expert-checked claims from 40 medical-agent answers (drawn from 281 real traces), experts marked 139 claims as should-not-pass and ProvenanceGuard caught 138, letting only one through.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Near-complete recall on unsupported claims is the key proof point for safety-critical deployments.
insights.quote: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through.

insights.claim: ProvenanceGuard's conservative setting also held 67 claims experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair, trading false positives for fewer missed unsupported claims.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: False-positive rate implies added human-review cost in production.
insights.quote: It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair.

insights.claim: ProvenanceGuard achieved a reject/block F1 of 0.802 versus MiniCheck 0.783, RAGAS Faithfulness 0.758, AlignScore 0.662 and SummaC-ZS 0.436, and was the only verifier emitting claim-to-source IDs.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Modest F1 lead over MiniCheck; the differentiation is source attribution rather than raw accuracy.

insights.claim: For claims with an identifiable source, ProvenanceGuard selected the correct source about 86% of the time in the main test.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Quantifies attribution accuracy, the system's core differentiator.
insights.quote: it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

insights.claim: In a harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard reached 0.846 block F1 but identified the exact source in only 50.3% of claims, which the authors flag as an area for improvement.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Distinguishing near-duplicate sources remains unsolved, limiting reliability in dense enterprise data environments.
insights.quote: identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims.
insights.locator: Checking claims when sources look similar

insights.claim: In a controlled test where the named source was swapped in 50 cases with evidence intact, ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Shows reliable detection of clear misattribution.

insights.claim: The repair loop resolved all 173 blocked answers in the full-trace run, but 144 ended in fallback text rather than substantive rewrites; on reconstructed multi-source traces it resolved all 59 blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: High fallback rate on real traces means verification often reduces answer usefulness rather than fixing it.
insights.quote: 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite

insights.claim: As an offline gate, ProvenanceGuard adds roughly half a second per answer on the local configuration, with NLI and routing calls in the tens of milliseconds.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Low latency overhead makes source-aware verification economically viable as a release gate.
insights.quote: roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration

insights.claim: NVIDIA NVFlow merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent that uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware approach to check answers against retrieved SEC excerpts without changing rollouts or training data.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Early adoption in an NVIDIA project signals traction for provenance verification in financial AI agents.
insights.quote: NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent.

insights.claim: Multiverse Computing positions ProvenanceGuard as a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment, extensible beyond medicine to any agent that logs tools and sources.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Indicates Multiverse Computing's push into agent verification/guardrails for regulated enterprises.

insights.claim: Replying to a reader, author Ander Alvarez Sanz acknowledged the paper has no direct comparison against a cheaper source-aware LLM judge, arguing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources.
insights.speaker: Ander Alvarez Sanz
insights.so_what: Open question whether specialized verification pipelines beat simple second-LLM-call judges on cost and accuracy.
insights.quote: A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own.
